answer:
Using Heisenberg's uncertainty principle for position and momentum: $\Delta x \cdot \Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}$.

For an electron to reside inside a nucleus, the maximum uncertainty in position is the nuclear radius, $\Delta x \approx 10^{-14}\text{ m}$.

The minimum momentum is $\Delta p \approx \frac{\hbar}{2 \Delta x} \approx \frac{1.054 \times 10^{-34}}{2 \times 10^{-14}} \approx 5.27 \times 10^{-21}\text{ kg m/s}$.

The corresponding kinetic energy for a relativistic electron is $E_k \approx pc \approx (5.27 \times 10^{-21})(3 \times 10^8)\text{ J} \approx 10\text{ MeV}$. 

Since beta decay experiments show nuclear electrons would only possess $\sim 2\text{--}3\text{ MeV}$, electrons cannot reside inside the nucleus.
